simple: how hard something twists.
analogy: how hard Amara presses on the pedal.
precise: the turning effect of a force about an axis, force times lever arm, in newton metres (N m). A wheel of radius r pushing the ground with force F needs torque F × r.
source: D1 of F9-08 (Austin Hughes, Bill Drury, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many turns of the motor make one turn of the wheel.
analogy: the bicycle's gears, used the other way round: a robot uses a large ratio to turn a fast, weak motor into a slow, strong wheel.
precise: for a ratio G, wheel speed = motor speed / G and wheel torque = G × motor torque × gearbox efficiency (efficiency below 1 because of friction in the gears).
source: D1 of F9-08 (Austin Hughes, Bill Drury, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the twist the motor can keep up without getting too hot.
analogy: the effort Amara can keep up on a long hill.
precise: the torque at which the motor's temperature stays within its limit in continuous running, given in the motor's datasheet; brief peaks above it are allowed only for times the datasheet states.
source: D1 of F9-08 (Austin Hughes, Bill Drury, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications"); D2 of F9-08 (The datasheets of the gearmotor, gearhead, hobby servo, stepper motor, stepper driver and brushless controller chosen for the course robot) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a motor that moves in small fixed steps, one step per pulse.
analogy: climbing stairs one step at a time instead of walking up a ramp.
precise: a motor whose rotor lines up with the magnetic field of whichever coils are energised; switching the coil currents in a fixed sequence turns it by one step per change, so position is known by counting steps, as long as no step is lost.
source: D1 of F9-08 (Austin Hughes, Bill Drury, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making smaller steps between the big ones.
analogy: taking half or quarter stairs.
precise: a driver mode that sets the two coil currents to intermediate values so the rotor rests between full-step positions; the driver's datasheet lists the available divisions.
source: D2 of F9-08 (The datasheets of the gearmotor, gearhead, hobby servo, stepper motor, stepper driver and brushless controller chosen for the course robot) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the motor misses steps it was told to make, and nobody notices.
analogy: tripping on the stairs while still counting steps out loud.
precise: when the torque needed to follow the step sequence exceeds what the motor can produce at that step rate, the rotor falls out of step with the field; an open-loop controller keeps counting, so its position belief becomes wrong.
source: D1 of F9-08 (Austin Hughes, Bill Drury, "Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far apart the two drive wheels are.
analogy: the width of the bicycle's handlebar, if each hand were a wheel.
precise: the distance b between the contact points of the left and right wheels on the floor, used to turn the difference in wheel distances into a change of heading.
source: D1 of F9-09 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017; tier 3): wheeled mobile robots, differenti) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an error that happens the same way every time, because a number is wrong.
analogy: kwame measured the wheel with a stretched string.
precise: errors from imperfect kinematic parameters (unequal or mis-measured wheel diameters, wrong track width, misalignment); they push the estimate in the same direction on every run and grow steadily with distance.
source: D3 of F9-09 (Johann Borenstein, Liqiang Feng, "Measurement and Correction of Systematic Odometry Errors in Mobile Robots" (IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation; tier) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an error that happens now and then, when a wheel slides or bumps.
analogy: the back wheel spinning in the mud.
precise: errors from the interaction with the floor (slip while accelerating or turning, uneven floors, bumps); they depend on where and how the robot drove, not on a parameter.
source: D3 of F9-09 (Johann Borenstein, Liqiang Feng, "Measurement and Correction of Systematic Odometry Errors in Mobile Robots" (IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation; tier) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: measuring the robot's real wheel sizes and wheel spacing by test drives.
analogy: kwame rolling his bicycle along a measured 10 m line and counting turns.
precise: estimating the effective wheel diameters and track width from drives whose true result is measured (straight runs, turns in place, closed square paths in both directions), then using those values in the odometry.
source: D3 of F9-09 (Johann Borenstein, Liqiang Feng, "Measurement and Correction of Systematic Odometry Errors in Mobile Robots" (IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation; tier) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the directions printed on the IMU chip or board.
analogy: the way your inner ear happens to sit in your head.
precise: the frame in which the sensor reports its measurements, defined by the axis markings in its datasheet; it is fixed to the robot but generally rotated (and offset) from the body frame.
source: D3 of F9-10 (The datasheet of the IMU chosen for the course robot) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: finding out exactly how the IMU sits on the robot, by measuring.
analogy: standing still to feel which way is down, then walking forward to feel which way is ahead.
precise: estimating the sensor-to-body rotation from measurements with known motion: gravity at rest gives the body's up axis, a straight acceleration gives the forward axis.
source: D1 of F9-10 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: adding up small turns to know which way you face.
analogy: counting the turns of the swivel chair with your eyes closed.
precise: θ(t) = θ(0) + ∫ ωz dt, computed as a sum of rate × time step; any constant error in ωz adds an error that grows in proportion to time.
source: D1 of F9-10 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: measuring what the gyro says while the robot is truly still, and subtracting it.
analogy: noticing that you "feel" a slow turn even when the chair stands still, and ignoring that much from then on.
precise: averaging the gyroscope output over a window during which the robot is known not to rotate, and using the mean as the bias estimate; valid only if the robot really is still during the window.
source: D1 of F9-10 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D4 of F9-10 (Oliver J. Woodman, "An introduction to inertial navigation" (University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory technical report; tier 5): gyro error sources (constant) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one full sweep of distances, one per direction, in a flat slice around the robot.
analogy: nadia's lamp sweeping once round.
precise: a list of ranges ri measured at beam angles θi = θmin + i·Δθ in the sensor's plane, with a timestamp, valid range limits and the sensor's frame.
source: D1 of F9-11 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics"); D2 of F9-11 (The datasheet, protocol description and driver documentation of the 2D LiDAR chosen for the course robot) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many degrees lie between two neighbouring beams.
analogy: how far Nadia moves the lamp between two looks.
precise: the angle increment Δθ between consecutive beams; at range r the gap between neighbouring spots is about r·Δθ (Δθ in radians), so thin objects far away can fall between beams.
source: D1 of F9-11 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: where the LiDAR sits on the robot and which way it faces.
analogy: the lamp is on the handlebar, not on Nadia's nose.
precise: the position (x, y) and yaw of the sensor frame in the robot's body frame, used to move every scan point into the body frame; part of the robot's description of its sensors (RB301, F9-29).
source: D5 of F9-11 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017; tier 3): rigid-body transforms in the plan) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a file that stores sensor messages with their times, so you can play them back later.
analogy: a diary of every sweep of the lamp.
precise: a time-stamped recording of sensor data in a defined format; ROS 2 records "bags" with its own tools (RB303); this course uses a small text format of its own, described in Listing 1, so that it can be read without ROS 2.
source: D4 of F9-11 (ROS 2 documentation (Open Robotics and the ROS 2 community; tier 2): the sensor message for planar scans and the bag recording tools. Title only) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a scan looks bent because the robot moved while the sweep was going on.
analogy: the kerb looking bent because Nadia turned while sweeping.
precise: the beams of one scan are measured at different times during the sweep; if the robot moves or turns during it, treating them as simultaneous misplaces points; de-skewing corrects each beam with the robot's motion at its own time.
source: D1 of F9-11 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

term: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)
simple: how big each picture is, how each dot is stored, and how many pictures per second.
analogy: how sharp, how colourful and how often Joon's eyes send pictures.
precise: a combination of width × height in pixels, an encoding of each pixel (for example 8-bit grey, 16-bit YUV-type, 24-bit RGB, or a compressed format) and frames per second; the camera supports a fixed list of modes, given in its datasheet.
source: D3 of F9-12 (The datasheet and driver documentation of the camera and depth camera chosen for the course robot) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many bytes per second the camera sends.
analogy: how much the eyes ask the brain to look at each second.
precise: width × height × bytes per pixel × frames per second for an uncompressed mode; it must fit the link (with its protocol overhead) and the computer's processing budget.
source: D1 of F9-12 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)

simple: how wide the camera sees, as an angle.
analogy: how far to the side Joon can see without turning his head.
precise: the angle covered by the image across its width (horizontal FOV); in the pinhole model, f = (W/2) / tan(FOV/2), with f the focal length in pixels and W the width in pixels.
source: D2 of F9-12 (Richard Hartley, Andrew Zisserman, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)

simple: smearing in a picture because something moved while the picture was taken.
analogy: the fruit stalls blurring as Joon rides past.
precise: the image of a point moving across the sensor during the exposure time t covers about (image speed in px/s) × t pixels; turning at ω rad/s gives about f·ω·t pixels near the centre.
source: D1 of F9-12 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)

simple: a camera whose picture says how far away each dot is.
analogy: joon's two eyes telling him the child is nearer than the stall.
precise: a sensor that outputs a depth image (a distance per pixel), by stereo matching, structured light or time of flight (F1-67); for stereo, Z = f·B/d with baseline B and disparity d, so a fixed disparity error gives a depth error growing with Z².
source: D2 of F9-12 (Richard Hartley, Andrew Zisserman, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)

simple: lining up the depth picture with the colour picture, dot by dot.
analogy: knowing which thing you see in colour is the one you feel is close.
precise: mapping each depth pixel to a 3D point, transforming it by the extrinsic transform between the two cameras, and projecting it into the colour camera; because the cameras are apart, the shift depends on distance (parallax).
source: D2 of F9-12 (Richard Hartley, Andrew Zisserman, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)

simple: how old a picture is by the time the robot acts on it.
analogy: joon's pictures arriving late.
precise: time from the moment of exposure to the moment a result computed from that image is available; measured with timestamps taken at capture and at result, on one clock.
source: D1 of F9-12 (Richard Szeliski, "Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Camera mode (resolution, pixel format, frame rate)

simple: a drawing of where the electricity goes, from the battery to every part.
analogy: how the food Joon ate reaches his legs, heart and brain.
precise: a diagram of the power path from source to loads: protection, switches, the emergency-stop path, converters and rails, with the current each branch carries.
source: D1 of F9-13 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one supply voltage shared by several parts, such as "5 V".
analogy: one pipe in a house's water system that several taps hang on.
precise: a supply net at one nominal voltage, fed by one source or converter, with a maximum continuous current set by that source and by its wiring.
source: D1 of F9-13 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part that makes a lower voltage by burning off the difference as heat.
analogy: braking on a downhill to keep a fixed speed: the extra energy becomes heat.
precise: a regulator that drops (Vin − Vout) across a pass transistor; it dissipates about (Vin − Vout) × Iout, so its efficiency is at most Vout/Vin; low noise, simple.
source: D1 of F9-13 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part that changes voltage by switching very quickly and storing energy in a coil, wasting little.
analogy: changing gear instead of braking.
precise: a converter that switches the input at a high frequency through an inductor and smooths the result; a buck converter steps down, a boost converter steps up; efficiency depends on load and is given as curves in its datasheet; it makes switching noise.
source: D1 of F9-13 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F9-13 (The datasheets of the chosen regulators and motor drivers) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a circuit in or beside the battery that switches it off if something unsafe happens.
analogy: joon's legs refusing to push when he is too tired.
precise: a protection circuit or battery management system (BMS) that disconnects the pack on under-voltage, over-voltage, over-current, short circuit or over-temperature, with thresholds and delays given by the pack maker.
source: D3 of F9-13 (The datasheet and safety instructions of the battery pack chosen for the course robot) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: voltage lost in the wires themselves.
analogy: pressure lost in a long, thin hose.
precise: ΔV = I × Rwire for the whole loop (out and back); Rwire = resistance per metre (from the wire's table) × loop length; it also heats the wire with I²R.
source: D1 of F9-13 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the switch that takes power away from the motors when the red button is pressed.
analogy: joon's hands on the brakes, which work even if his mind is elsewhere.
precise: a hardware path that removes energy from the actuators without depending on software (F9-07); which parts stay powered (for example the computer, to log the event) is a design decision written into the power tree.
source: S1 of F9-13 (University Authoring Guide, section "Honesty first" and the F9 faculty safety rules)

simple: how much of the time a bus is busy carrying messages.
analogy: how much of the time somebody is talking on the team radio.
precise: the sum over all message streams of (bits per message, including protocol overhead) × (messages per second), divided by the bus's bit rate; a design keeps it below a chosen limit so that delays stay short and there is room for growth.
source: D2 of F9-14 (ISO 11898-1 and Bosch "CAN Specification 2.0") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: on CAN, the message with the smaller number wins when two start together.
analogy: the more urgent call keeps the radio channel.
precise: during arbitration, nodes send their identifiers bit by bit; a dominant 0 overrides a recessive 1, so the lowest identifier wins without being damaged and the others retry when the bus is next idle (F1-47); identifiers therefore set message priority for the whole bus.
source: D2 of F9-14 (ISO 11898-1 and Bosch "CAN Specification 2.0") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the longest a single CAN message can take on the wire.
analogy: the longest one call on the radio can last.
precise: for a classical CAN data frame with an 11-bit identifier and n data bytes, the bits of the frame plus the inter-frame space plus the most stuff bits the data could cause; this build's model uses 8n + 47 + ⌊(34 + 8n − 1)/4⌋ bits, 135 bits for 8 bytes (unverified, see the box).
source: D3 of F9-14 (Robert I. Davis, Alan Burns, Reinder J. Bril, Johan J. Lukkien, "Controller Area Network (CAN) schedulability analysis: Refuted, revisited and revised", Real-Ti) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a message that never gets a turn because others always win.
analogy: the leader's "turn left" never finding a gap.
precise: on a priority-arbitrated bus that is fully loaded by higher-priority traffic, a lower-priority message waits indefinitely; unlike a slow bus, the delay is unbounded.
source: D3 of F9-14 (Robert I. Davis, Alan Burns, Reinder J. Bril, Johan J. Lukkien, "Controller Area Network (CAN) schedulability analysis: Refuted, revisited and revised", Real-Ti) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a device stops on its own if commands stop arriving.
analogy: a rider who stops pedalling if he has heard nothing from the leader for too long.
precise: a receiver-side watchdog: if no valid command message has arrived within a stated time, the receiver goes to a safe state (for a motor driver: stop) and reports it; the timeout is longer than the command period by a chosen margin.
source: S1 of F9-14 (University Authoring Guide, section "Honesty first" and the F9 faculty safety rules)

simple: resistors at the ends of a long bus cable that stop signals from bouncing back.
analogy: soft walls at the ends of a tunnel so that echoes do not drown the voice.
precise: resistors matching the cable's characteristic impedance placed at both physical ends of a differential bus such as CAN; their value and placement come from the bus standard and the transceiver's datasheet.
source: D1 of F9-14 (NXP Semiconductors, "I2C-bus specification and user manual" (UM10204)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the way Linux lets a program send and receive CAN messages like network packets.
analogy: the radio's headset that plugs into the computer.
precise: the Linux CAN subsystem: CAN interfaces appear as network interfaces (for example can0), and a program opens a socket of family PF_CAN, type SOCK_RAW, protocol CAN_RAW, binds it to the interface and reads and writes struct can_frame (declared in linux/can.h).
source: D5 of F9-14 (Linux kernel UAPI headers linux/can.h and linux/can/raw.h (package linux-libc-dev 6.8.0-146.146)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a written list of every part, every wire and every power line of the robot, with the numbers that show it works.
analogy: the club's check list for each bicycle.
precise: a design document listing parts, rails, connections (nets), buses and addresses, each with the datasheet values that justify it and their citations, together with the checks performed; it sits between the block diagram and the schematic (F1-79).
source: S1 of F9-15 (University Authoring Guide, section "Honesty first" (every claim with a source) and the F9 faculty safety rules)

simple: whether the "high" and "low" of one chip are understood as "high" and "low" by the next.
analogy: whether one rider's hand signals are big enough for the next rider to read.
precise: a driver's guaranteed output levels must fall inside the receiver's guaranteed input levels: VOH(min) ≥ VIH(min) and VOL(max) ≤ VIL(max), with margin for noise and ground offset; and the driver's highest output must not exceed the receiver's absolute maximum input.
source: D1 of F9-15 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small circuit that translates a signal from one voltage to another.
analogy: an interpreter between two riders who signal differently.
precise: a translator IC, a transistor circuit or (for slow, one-way signals into a lower-voltage input) a resistor divider, chosen for direction, speed and the voltages on both sides from its datasheet.
source: D1 of F9-15 (Paul Horowitz, Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D2 of F9-15 (The datasheets of the course kit's parts) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two devices on one I2C bus answering to the same number.
analogy: two riders with the same name on the team radio.
precise: two targets with the same 7-bit address on one bus both respond and their answers collide; fixed by an address-select pin (if the part has one), a second bus, or a bus multiplexer.
source: D3 of F9-15 (NXP Semiconductors, "I2C-bus specification and user manual" (UM10204)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a team's own rule for keeping well below a limit.
analogy: the club's rule to ride at most 80 % of your top speed downhill.
precise: a stated margin applied to datasheet limits, such as loading a rail to at most 80 % of its regulator's maximum continuous current or a bus to at most 70 % (F9-14); it is a team decision written into the plan, not a property of any part.
source: S1 of F9-15 (University Authoring Guide, section "Honesty first" (every claim with a source) and the F9 faculty safety rules)

simple: writing down exactly where a number came from.
analogy: "tyre pressure from the tyre's sidewall", not "about right".
precise: for each value in the plan, the document (part number, revision) and the table or section it was copied from, so that a reviewer can check it and the plan can be updated when a part changes.
source: S1 of F9-15 (University Authoring Guide, section "Honesty first" (every claim with a source) and the F9 faculty safety rules)
